insights.title: Insights
insights.intro: Short notes from our partners. General information, not advice.

items.title: Lasting powers of attorney, while you can
items.author: sophie-lund
items.summary: Why to choose the people who may one day decide for you, and to do it before you need to.
body: A lasting power of attorney lets you choose who can make decisions for you if you can no longer make them yourself. There are two kinds: one for property and money, and one for health and welfare.

It must be registered with the Office of the Public Guardian before it can be used, and registration takes time. Making it while you are well means the people you trust can act straight away when they need to.
We talk through who to choose, whether they act together or separately, and any instructions you want to give them.

photo.alt: A desk lamp lit beside a pile of old books

items.title: Living together without marrying
items.author: eleanor-pryce
items.summary: Couples who live together have fewer automatic rights than married couples. A cohabitation agreement and a will can fill the gap.
body: Many couples assume that living together for years gives them the same rights as marriage. In England and Wales it does not.
If one partner dies without a will, the other may not inherit automatically. If the relationship ends, what each owns depends largely on whose name it is in.
A cohabitation agreement records what you have agreed about your home and money, and a will says what should happen on death. Both are simple to make and much harder to argue about later.

photo.alt: A vaulted corridor with a single hanging lamp

items.title: Your digital life, in your will
items.author: sophie-lund

photo.alt: A row of lamps along a library table

items.summary: Online accounts, photographs and digital money are part of what you leave. A little preparation saves your executors months.
body: Much of what we own now lives online: bank and investment accounts, photographs, email, and sometimes digital currencies. Your executors can only deal with what they can find.
Keep a private list of your accounts and where they are held, and tell your executors where to find it. Don't put passwords in your will: once probate is granted, a will becomes a public document.
Some services let you name a person to manage your account after your death. We can help you decide who should deal with your digital life, and write it into your will.

items.title: Leaving a gift to charity
items.author: hugo-ashdown

photo.alt: A tall window between dark bookshelves in an old library

items.summary: A gift to charity in your will can carry on what mattered to you, and can reduce the inheritance tax on the rest of the estate.
body: Gifts to registered charities in a will are generally free of inheritance tax. Leaving a large enough share of the estate to charity can also lower the rate of tax on the rest.
The wording matters. A gift should name the charity precisely, with its registered number, and say what should happen if it has merged or closed by the time the gift is made.
If you would rather your family chose the charities, a letter of wishes alongside a gift to a family foundation or a trust can give them that role.

items.title: When a will is challenged
items.author: imogen-carr

photo.alt: A brass lion-head knocker on a dark wooden door

items.summary: Why wills are challenged, and why it pays to act early if you think a will is wrong, or if yours may be questioned.
body: A will can be challenged because the person who made it lacked the capacity to understand it, was put under pressure, or because it was not signed and witnessed properly.

Separately, close family and dependants who were not reasonably provided for can ask a court for provision from the estate. Those claims usually have to be made within six months of the grant of probate.
Most disputes are settled without a trial, often through mediation. Taking advice early, before positions harden, is the quietest way through.

items.title: Buying a leasehold flat: what we check
items.author: marcus-hale

photo.alt: A brass knocker and keyhole on an open wooden door

items.summary: With a leasehold flat you buy a lease, not the building. These are the points we look at before you commit.
body: We start with the years left on the lease. A short lease can be costly to extend and harder to sell or mortgage later, so we check it first.
Then the money: the ground rent, how it can rise, and the service charge, with any large works the building is planning that you may be asked to pay towards.
Finally the rules: what the lease lets you do (renovating, letting, keeping a pet) and how well the building is managed. We set all of it out in one report before you exchange contracts.

guides.title: Guides for families
guides.intro: Longer pieces on the decisions families make, reviewed by a partner.

items.title: A will when you own property abroad
items.author: hugo-ashdown
items.summary: Owning a home in another country can mean more than one set of rules decides what happens to it.
body: Property abroad is often governed by the law of the country where it is, not only by English law. Some countries have rules about who must inherit.
One will may not be enough. Many families have a will in England and another in the country where the property is, written so that neither cancels the other.
We work with lawyers in the other country so the two fit together, and we keep a note of where each will is kept.

photo.alt: A window opening onto a garden from a dark library

items.title: Choosing trustees
items.author: sophie-lund
items.summary: The people who run a trust matter as much as its terms. What to think about before you name them.
body: Trustees make the decisions a trust leaves open, sometimes for decades. They need judgement, time and the confidence of the family.
Families often choose a mix: someone who knows the family well, and someone independent who can hold the line when needed.
You can also leave a letter of wishes, which trustees read alongside the trust. It is not binding, but it tells them what you would want.

photo.alt: A brass desk lamp in a library

items.title: Being an executor
items.author: sophie-lund

photo.alt: Shelves of old books with a library ladder

items.summary: What it means to be named in someone's will to deal with their estate, and how much of it you can ask us to do.
body: An executor gathers in what the person owned, pays what they owed, and passes the rest to the people named in the will. It can take a year or more.
You don't have to do it alone, or at all. You can ask a solicitor to do the work for you, and if you haven't yet started to act you can usually step aside formally.
Executors can be personally responsible if they pay out too early and a debt appears later. Notices placed before the estate is distributed help protect you, and we place them as a matter of course.

items.title: Passing on a family company
items.author: daniel-okoro

photo.alt: A carved panelled door with a lion-head knocker

items.summary: How shares in a family company can pass to the next generation, and the documents that keep it running in the meantime.
body: A family company passes on through its shares. Who receives them, and when, is set by your will and by the company's own rules: its articles and any shareholders' agreement.
The rules should say what happens if a shareholder dies, divorces or wants to leave, so that shares stay in the family and decisions can still be made.
Some business assets may qualify for relief from inheritance tax. The rules have changed recently, so we check the current position with your accountant before you decide.

items.title: An agreement before you marry
items.author: eleanor-pryce

photo.alt: A tall arched window in a dark, empty room

items.summary: What a prenuptial agreement can do in England and Wales, and how to make one a court is likely to respect.
body: A prenuptial agreement records how you would divide what you own if the marriage ended. In England and Wales it is not automatically binding, but courts give real weight to a fair agreement both people entered freely.
Three things help most: signing well before the wedding, each of you taking your own legal advice, and both of you setting out fully what you own.
An agreement can be reviewed later, after children or a change in fortunes, so that it stays fair to both of you.

items.title: Buying a house in London
items.author: marcus-hale

photo.alt: A lantern beside the doorway of a white town house

items.summary: The stages from offer to keys, what can slow them down, and what we need from you along the way.
body: Once your offer is accepted we check the title, order searches and raise questions with the seller's solicitor. A survey and your mortgage offer run alongside.
When everything is clear, contracts are exchanged and you are committed; completion, when the money moves and you get the keys, usually follows a week or two later.
After completion we register you as the owner and file the Stamp Duty Land Tax return, which is due within 14 days.

glossary.title: Words we use
glossary.intro: The legal words you may meet, each in one plain sentence.

terms.means: The person named in a will to deal with the estate.
The person who deals with an estate when there is no will, or no executor who can act.
The court document that lets executors collect and deal with what the person owned.
Everything a person owned when they died, less what they owed.
Someone who receives something under a will or a trust.
An arrangement where trustees hold money or property for the benefit of others.
A person who looks after a trust and makes its decisions.
A private note to your trustees or executors saying what you would like; it guides them but does not bind them.
A document choosing who can make decisions for you if you can't, registered with the Office of the Public Guardian.
Dying without a valid will; the law then decides who inherits.
A cost we pay to someone else on your behalf, such as a court fee, charged at cost.
The moment a property sale becomes binding on both sides.
The day the money moves and the keys are handed over.
Owning a property for a fixed number of years under a lease, rather than outright.
Our check that we don't already act for anyone on the other side, before you tell us about your matter.
